summary:
The Quiet After is a 3D website that brings retired space machines back to life. It sparks the imagination of young kids while still giving older students the real facts they want.
The site makes complex space history easy to enjoy for all ages. It pairs 3D maps with "My Space Diary"- short, first-person stories where each spacecraft tells its own tale.
Using official NASA photos, videos, and records, the website shares key details like launch dates, locations, and how long each mission lasted. Its clean design keeps younger learners from feeling overwhelmed without boring older space fans. Hosted on Vercel, The Quiet After turns silent, forgotten spacecraft into living stories of human exploration.
details:
What Does Our Project Do and How Does It Work?

The Quiet After is an interactive 3D web platform and mobile-friendly exploration game that brings 15 of NASA’s retired and discarded off-world spacecraft back to life for school-age learners (ages 6 and up) and space enthusiasts.

From an intuitive main menu, users choose between three distinct 3D environments:

  • The Moon (Cesium ion 3D Globe): Renders a high-resolution 3D lunar surface featuring 4 historic artifacts placed at their exact real-world landing coordinates. Users can orbit, zoom, and click any marker to smoothly focus the camera and choose between "Read My Full Story" or (for 3 of the 4 lunar sites) "Game: Land on Site."
  • Mars (Cesium ion 3D Globe): Offers the same precision orbital exploration tailored to the Martian landscape, showcasing 6 iconic rovers and landers at their true geological resting places, with 4 of the 6 sites playable in "Game: Land on Site."
  • Deep Space (Three.js 3D Solar System): Loads an interactive 3D model of the solar system paired with a chronological timeline along the bottom. Users can scrub through mission eras to visit 5 deep-space probes along their real orbital trajectories and open their full stories.

Each artifact features two core modes of engagement:

  • "Read My Full Story" (Interactive Mission Profile): Opens a dedicated story page containing official NASA photography, curated videos from NASA’s official YouTube channel, verified mission specifications, and an engaging narrative written from the perspective of the hardware itself.
  • "Game: Land on Site" (3D Surface Exploration Game): Drops players directly onto the lunar or Martian surface beside the spacecraft across 7 playable flagship missions (3 on the Moon, 4 on Mars). Guided by optional voice narration that can be skipped at any time, players can walk, jump, use a flashlight to illuminate hardware details, complete an interactive discovery checklist, and inspect individual components up close to learn what each instrument did and what science it made possible.

 What Value Does Our Project Add?

  • Turns Technical Archives into Accessible Stories: Most records of retired spacecraft sit in dense engineering logs and text-heavy databases. The Quiet After translates authentic NASA coordinates, hardware specs, and mission histories into interactive visual storytelling built for young minds.
  • Connects Hardware Engineering to Real Science: By letting students walk up to a rover or lander and inspect individual instruments—such as cameras, spectrometers, solar arrays, or drills—the platform draws a clear, memorable link between how a machine was built and what discoveries it unlocked.
  • Instant Browser & Mobile Access: Hosted live on Vercel and optimized for both desktop and mobile devices, the entire platform—including the 3D surface game—runs directly in a phone or computer web browser with zero downloads, installations, or specialized hardware required.

What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

While active missions regularly capture headlines, dozens of pioneering machines sit silently on the Moon, on Mars, or coasting through deep space. Directly addressing the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge, The Quiet After aims to spark lasting curiosity in students as young as 6 years old by turning silent monuments of spaceflight into relatable explorers with stories to tell. By showing young learners how past robotic pioneers paved the way for today’s missions, the project inspires the next generation of scientists, engineers, and storytellers to see discarded space hardware as living history.

What are the Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software We Used?

  • Frontend & 3D Graphics: React, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, Cesium ion (for 3D lunar and Martian planetary terrain and exact coordinate mapping), and Three.js (for the 3D solar system timeline and playable 3D surface environments).
  • AI-Assisted Prototyping & Development: Google AI Studio and Claude Code for rapid full-stack prototyping, 3D scene integration, and iterative debugging.
  • Hosting & Version Control: GitHub and Vercel for version control and live, globally accessible web deployment.
  • Verified NASA Data & Media Sources: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) Master Catalog, NASA Open Data Portal, official NASA mission websites, archival imagery from NASA web galleries, and official mission videos from the NASA YouTube channel.

What Makes Our Project Creative?

  • First-Person Hardware Storytelling: Instead of presenting dry encyclopedia entries, each spacecraft narrates its own journey ("Read My Full Story"), giving cold metal and circuitry a distinct voice, purpose, and legacy.
  • Orbital-to-Surface Gameplay Loop: Users seamlessly transition from viewing a spacecraft’s exact spot on a 3D planetary globe to standing beside it on the surface—complete with a flashlight mechanic, jump physics, voice narration, and a gamified component-inspection checklist.
  • Tailored Visual Identity Across Environments: Each destination adapts its visual design and interaction model to match its setting—planetary globes for surface artifacts on the Moon and Mars, and an interactive orbital timeline for deep-space voyagers.

What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

  • Age-Appropriate UI/UX (Ages 8+): We designed an uncluttered, visually engaging interface with clear three-path navigation and interactive pop-up cards so children as young as 6 can navigate effortlessly without feeling overwhelmed, while keeping scientific details rich enough for older space enthusiasts.
  • Mobile-First Playability: Recognizing that many students access educational tools on smartphones rather than high-end computers, we specifically optimized the website and the 3D surface game controls for mobile screens so kids can play directly on their phones.
  • Self-Paced Accessibility: Voice narration during surface missions can be skipped at any moment, supporting both auditory learners who want a guided tour and independent readers who prefer exploring at their own speed.
  • Scientific Accuracy & Fact-Checking: Every landing coordinate, orbital path, mission timeline, and inspectable spacecraft component was cross-checked against official NSSDCA and NASA mission records.

How Is Our Project Different From Existing Ones?

  • Beyond Static NASA Catalogs & Textbooks: Existing archival databases offer authoritative data, but they lack visual immersion, narrative voice, and interactive mechanics tailored to elementary and middle-school learners.
  • Beyond Passive 3D Planet Viewers: Standard 3D space viewers only let users look at pins on a map from orbit. The Quiet After bridges planetary cartography, first-person storytelling, archival NASA videos, and a mobile-playable 3D surface inspection game in a single unified web app—letting kids actually land beside NASA’s forgotten explorers and inspect how they worked.
